tagline: Horse farms line a pike linking Paris Pike with Kentucky Horse Park.
intro: Ironworks Pike carries KY 1973 through horse-farm country north of Lexington, linking Paris Pike with the Kentucky Horse Park and I-75. Kentucky’s designated scenic corridor covers 7.187 miles from Paris Pike to the west end of I-75’s Exit 120 interchange. The Kentucky Horse Park combines a working farm, equestrian competitions and a museum of horse history. The full numbered highway extends through eastern and northern Lexington and into Scott County; the scenic designation applies to this shorter section of Ironworks Pike.

The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet records scenic designation on November 20, 1996. By then, Spindletop Hall had changed roles and the Kentucky Horse Park had opened. Spindletop Hall, built for Pansy Yount in the 1930s, became the University of Kentucky’s faculty, staff and alumni club in 1962. The Horse Park opened in 1978, and racing champion Forego arrived the following year.

For an eastward drive, start at I-75 and the Horse Park, then pass Spindletop Hall on Iron Works Pike. Continue across Newtown Pike and Russell Cave Road toward Paris Pike, reversing KY 1973’s northwestward course through the farms. Near the Paris Pike end, Elmendorf’s remaining marble pillars mark the site of a demolished mansion. The designated corridor ends at US 27/68, Paris Pike.

moments.title: Kentucky Horse Park
moments.text: Man o’ War lies beneath his own statue near the entrance to Kentucky Horse Park. The Thoroughbred won 20 of his 21 races before retiring to stud. He was first buried at Faraway Farm; his remains were moved here during the park’s establishment in the 1970s. Herbert Haseltine sculpted the memorial. Elsewhere in the park, Jim Reno’s life-size sculpture shows Secretariat with jockey Ron Turcotte aboard and groom Eddie Sweat leading him. The park opened in 1978 and houses the International Museum of the Horse, with a permanent collection of horse history and memorabilia.
moments.notice: Near the entrance, Man o’ War’s statue stands above his grave.

moments.title: Spindletop Hall
moments.text: Before Spindletop Hall, the Younts kept American Saddlebred horses in Beaumont, Texas. Pansy Yount established the farm in 1935 after the death of her husband, oilman Miles Franklin Yount. Construction of the mansion began that year and took two years. Its 40 rooms each had a thermostat; the house also contained 14 bathrooms and 11 fireplaces. On the Kentucky property, Pansy expanded the farm to 1,066 acres, with 18 barns and housing for servants and farmhands. Since 1962, the house has served as the University of Kentucky’s faculty, staff and alumni club.

moments.title: Elmendorf Farm
moments.text: Marble pillars survive at Elmendorf where James Ben Ali Haggin’s Green Hills mansion once stood. Haggin expanded the horse farm along Paris Pike and built the mansion on a hill overlooking Elk Horn. After his death in 1914, the estate was divided. Joseph Widener demolished the unoccupied mansion in 1929 to avoid its taxes, leaving the pillars. The original farm section retains historic barns and houses as well as the columns. Later divisions of Elmendorf created neighboring farms, including Normandy, where Man o’ War’s parents, Fair Play and Mahubah, are buried.
